claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is considered in the as-cast state.
As-cast HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing dual-phase regions and localized microstructural-property variations.
A random-forest surrogate incorporating variance-based descriptors will predict the mechanical response more accurately than conventional simulation methods.
The random-forest surrogate will generate predictions more rapidly than conventional finite-element or ab initio simulations.
Variance descriptors for atomic planar density, elastic moduli, and the D parameter can represent heterogeneity in a multicomponent alloy.
SEM, XRD, and EDS measurements can provide the local data needed to calculate atomic-packing, local-elasticity, and dislocation-parameter variance descriptors.
Local phase boundaries and grain orientations in the hierarchical heterostructure induce spatial variability in mechanical properties.
Spatial variability in local properties mediates the alloy's macroscopic response under load.
High variance in atomic planar density indicates nonuniform atomic packing that can produce localized weaknesses and reduced mechanical integrity.
High variance in elastic moduli indicates nonuniform stiffness and localized deformation under stress.
The D parameter reflects competition between dislocation emission and brittle fracture and is relevant to plasticity prediction.
Incorporating heterogeneity descriptors allows the surrogate to better resolve localized deformation, dislocation emission, and crack propagation.
The model will improve prediction of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior.
The model will reduce average prediction error for each targeted mechanical response by approximately 20–30%.
The conventional finite-element or ab initio baseline does not explicitly represent spatial variability caused by the hierarchical heterostructure.
The hypothesis may fail if heterostructure variability cannot be measured reliably.
The hypothesis may fail if the variance descriptors omit critical deformation or fracture mechanisms.
The hypothesis may fail if the training data do not span the microstructural variation present in HfNbTiVAl10.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20% for every measured property, or failure to reduce runtime by at least 50%, is declared falsifying.
